name: BitSerializer
workload: Fields per millisecond saving a C++ test model (array of objects with 10 fields each: bool, int8, uint64, float, double and five strings including long, Russian Unicode, escaped and multi-line values) to an in-memory std::string and loading it back, MsgPack format; best (minimum) time over a 30 second window per stage, thread pinned to one core.
claimed_speedup: BitSerializer-MsgPack vs NlohmannJson-MsgPack: save to memory 86842 vs 2621 fields/ms (about 33x, derived from page data), load from memory 49254 vs 2206 fields/ms (about 22x, derived from page data). README also says the built-in JSON archive is about 40% faster than BitSerializer's own RapidJSON-based JSON archive, and that wrapped third-party formats (RapidJSON, PugiXml, RapidYAML) cost about 5% against their native APIs.
tradeoffs: Header-style C++17 library; types need a Serialize function or KeyValue mapping per class (non-intrusive). MsgPack, CSV and the new built-in JSON archive have no external dependencies; the RapidJSON, PugiXml and RapidYAML archives pull in those libraries. Streams straight to and from the model with no intermediate DOM, so it cannot do arbitrary DOM manipulation the way nlohmann::json can.
caveats: Benchmark source is public (benchmarks/archives, with a CMake target and competitors/*.h) but no compiler, flags or CPU model are stated anywhere in the repo or README, and the committed report JSON and chart carry no machine information, so it is a first-party result with partial methodology (tier C, not A). The only nlohmann::json row is MsgPack; there is no nlohmann JSON text row in the committed report. The baseline builds a nlohmann::json DOM and converts it, while BitSerializer maps the struct straight to bytes, which the README itself calls not entirely fair ('Serialization' vs 'Parser' classes). Output equivalence is not checked: the committed output-size report does not include the nlohmann MsgPack row. Against RapidJSON, PugiXml and RapidYAML the BitSerializer archives are within about 5% or slightly slower, not faster (RapidJson save 14103 vs 13636, load 11957 vs 11149 fields/ms), so the speedup claim holds only for MsgPack against nlohmann. The 33x and 22x ratios are derived from the report's two numbers.

name: bstring
baseline: C standard library char* string functions (strcpy, strcat, strchr, strstr, strcspn, memmove)
workload: Upstream Bstrlib's cbench.c example: operations per second for assignment, char extraction, scan, concatenation (250 appends of a 62 character string plus '!!' into one growing buffer) and replace, bstring C API against plain char* code. The same page also benchmarks upstream's C++ wrapper CBString against std::string with cppbench.cpp.
claimed_speedup: Bstrlib C API as percent of char* Clib speed (100% is parity), columns WATCOM C 11.0c / Visual C++ 6.0 / Intel C++ 6.0 / gcc 3.3.3 Cygwin / gcc 3.3.3 Power 4 SUSE: concatenation 21700% / 23700% / 21200% / 9260% / 3980%; assignment 182% / 198% / 218% / 89% / 91%; scan 214% / 125% / 159% / 209% / 89%; char extraction 95% / 96% / 101% / 102% / 113%; replace 147% / 114% / 125% / 101% / 86%. Same page, CBString over std::string: concatenation 187% (WATCOM + STL port), 21100% (Visual C++ 6.0), 19400% (Intel C++ 6.0), 1330% (g++ 3.3.3 Cygwin), 200% (g++ 3.3.3 Power 4); char extraction 63% to 132%; replace 95% to 144%.
compiler_and_flags: WATCOM C/C++ 11.0c, Visual C++ 6.0 (12.00.8168), Intel C++ 6.0 (4.0 99026), gcc 3.3.3 on Cygwin and on SUSE Linux. The page states only that the compiler must be set to 'a reasonable maximum performance setting'; the makefiles shipped in examples-09282006.zip use gcc -O3, MSVC /O2 and Intel /Ox /Ob2 but the page does not say these were the flags used.
hardware: Athlon XP 1.620GHz (all Windows/Cygwin columns); Power 4 1GHz (SUSE Linux column)
stars_or_usage: 175 stars (msteinert fork); upstream websnarf/bstrlib 570 stars; packaged in many distributions per the README's repology badge
tradeoffs: Length-prefixed string struct (slen, mlen, data) that stays NUL-terminated for interop with char* code, so length is O(1) and appends amortize, at the cost of a header and a different API from <string.h>. Dual licensed BSD-3-Clause or GPL-2.0 (user's choice). This fork is pure C: it removed upstream's C++ wrapper (CBString, bstrwrap) and the const_bstring type, and adds Meson build, Check tests, fuzzing and CI.
caveats: The numbers are for upstream Bstrlib (websnarf/bstrlib, last commit 2016-11-02), measured with 2000s era compilers on a 1.62GHz Athlon XP and a 1GHz Power 4; the msteinert fork is described as binary compatible but was not re-benchmarked, and the CBString versus std::string rows apply only to upstream because the fork dropped the C++ wrapper. First-party project page with percentages only (no raw ops/s), flags not stated for the run, so tier C. The large concatenation ratios come from the baseline calling strcat repeatedly on a growing buffer (rescanning the whole string every call, quadratic) while bstring tracks length; a C program that keeps its own length would not lose this much. In cbench.c the char* scan test searches TESTSTRING1 while the bstring scan test searches a different, shorter string ('Dot. 123. Some more data.'). The std::string comparison used old STLs (WATCOM STL port, Visual C++ 6.0, g++ 3.3.3 libstdc++) and resets the accumulator with accum = "", which those implementations may treat differently from CBString; std::string was faster or equal in several rows (char extraction 63-132%, replace 95-144%) and the C API loses on assignment and replace in some columns (89%, 91%, 86%). The fork's own README and comparisons.md claim 'improved overall performance of common string operations' and an advantage over std::string at least as large as the Str library's, with no numbers.
